text: Patients arrive at a two-room clinic after long drives, often sick, often with a child in tow, and fill in a paper form that asks the same question three ways. The intake should take the questions to them one at a time, in plain words, on a borrowed tablet, so the nurse gets a history she can trust and the patient feels expected rather than processed.

A volunteer-run library lends drills, ladders and pressure washers, and today the catalogue is a spreadsheet only two people understand. Design is needed so a neighbour can see what exists, what is out, and how to borrow it without phoning anyone, and so the library feels like a shared shed, not a rental counter.

project: Grant reporting for a small foundation
text: Grantees spend days each year rewriting the same outcomes into our report template, and we read them looking for two numbers. The report should ask for what we actually use, show grantees what we did with last year's answers, and make honesty about a failed program feel safe to write down.

Dispatchers juggle forty trucks across three screens and a phone, and the cost of a missed exception is a load sitting at a dock overnight. The console has to make the one truck that needs attention impossible to miss and keep the thirty-nine that are fine quietly out of the way.

The shop's character is its staff picks and handwritten shelf cards, and none of that survives on the current site, which looks like every other storefront. The site should feel like walking in: opinionated recommendations first, events second, the catalogue third, with ordering simple enough that nobody gives up and buys elsewhere.

Residents applying for a fence or a deck permit cannot tell whether their application is moving, so they call the office, and the calls slow the office down. Design should show every applicant where their permit is, who has it, and what happens next, in language a first-time homeowner understands.

Newcomers want to practise the local language with people, not drills, and local volunteers want to help but do not know where to start. The app should pair them for short, low-stakes conversations, protect the newcomer's privacy completely, and never make anyone feel graded.

Our audience is ageing and the younger people who do come say the programme reads like a legal notice. The season should be presented as a set of evenings worth looking forward to, each with a reason to come, while keeping the subscribers who love the composer-and-opus listings.

project: Lab inventory for a university research group
text: Reagents expire on shelves because nobody knows who ordered them, and students reorder what is already in the freezer. The inventory needs to be faster to update than ignoring it, readable from a phone in a glove, and clear about what is dangerous before it is clear about what is cheap.

My grandmother's recipes live on stained index cards in three households, and the cousins argue about which version is real. The archive should keep every version side by side with who wrote it and when, feel warm rather than clinical, and make it easy for the youngest cousin to add the card she found.

Technicians climb turbines only in safe weather windows, and planning those climbs across a hundred turbines is done on a whiteboard. Design is needed to show the weather window, the crew and the fault list together so a planner can commit a day in minutes and a technician knows why they are on that tower.

Our members chose us because we are local and human, and our app feels like it was bought from a vendor, because it was. The app should do the everyday things fast and make the human parts visible: a named advisor, plain fees, and a way to talk to someone who knows the member's history.

Visitors carry their phones through the galleries but the current guide asks them to type object numbers and then stare at a screen. The guide should let people look at the art, not the phone, offering a story when they pause and staying silent when they move on.

New contributors read the docs, fail to build the project, and leave without telling us. The documentation should get someone from clone to a passing test in one sitting, say plainly what is unfinished, and make the people behind the project visible enough that asking a question feels allowed.

Volunteers sit with dying patients, and a missed shift means someone spends their last afternoon alone. Scheduling should make coverage gaps obvious to the coordinator days ahead, make swapping a shift easy without guilt, and respect that these volunteers are giving something heavy.

Shoppers wander the market looking for the one stall that sells duck eggs, and vendors move every week. The map should be the first thing people check on the walk over, show what is in season and who has it today, and give small vendors the same presence as the big ones.

After an outage we write a review document that nobody reads twice, and the same failure returns six months later. The tool should make the timeline and the decisions easy to reconstruct, keep blame out of the structure itself, and connect each review to the ones before it so patterns surface.

project: Children's reading tracker for a public library
text: The summer reading programme rewards pages read, and the kids who read slowly quit by July. The tracker should celebrate showing up and finishing, let a child see their own progress without comparing it to anyone else's, and give parents a reason to visit the library rather than just the app.

Our buildings are quiet and site-specific, and portfolio sites in our field shout with full-bleed renders. The portfolio should let the work breathe, show the context each building responds to, and read like the studio talks: slowly, precisely, with a point of view a client can disagree with.

Tenants in one building rarely know their neighbours share the same broken boiler and the same unanswered emails. The hub should make it safe to report a problem, show tenants they are not alone, and turn scattered complaints into a record the union can take to the landlord, without exposing anyone who is afraid.
